rows.name: multipart-pause-1500
rows.question: For exactly ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block, compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element. Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounds check. Explain the arithmetic.
rows.recognizedQuestion: For example, ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounce check Explain the arithmetic
rows.answer: You need 53 blocks. Since 10,000 = 52 × 192 + 16, the first 52 blocks cover 9,984 elements, and the final block has 16 active threads. In total, 53 × 192 = 10,176 threads are launched, leaving 176 outside the valid range. Interpreting “bounce check” as “bounds check,” all threads typically test index < 10,000, and those 176 extra threads fail the check and skip processing.

rows.name: switch-topic
rows.question: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.answer:
Snapshot isolation makes each transaction atomic, but it does not make concurrent transactions equivalent to running one after the other. Write skew occurs when both transactions read a snapshot that satisfies a shared invariant, then update different rows, so no write-write conflict forces either to abort.

For example, Alice and Bob are both on call, and at least one must remain. Each transaction sees both on call, checks that the other person is available, and marks its own person off call. Both can commit because they write different rows, leaving nobody on call. Atomicity prevents partial transactions; serializable isolation, or suitable locking that forces the checks to serialize, prevents this anomaly.

review.note: Atomicity contrasted with serialordering. ConcreteAlice/Bob readoldbothon, disjoint ownoffwrites bothcommit nobodyoncall, serialsecondremoval fails; proper coordination/isolationqualifier.
review.usefulPrefix: Snapshot isolation makes each transaction atomic, but it does not make concurrent transactions equivalent to running one after the other.
